key_terms.meaning: The single point through which the whole weight of a body acts, whatever way the body is turned: x̄ = ΣWx/ΣW.
The same weighted average taken with mass elements instead of weights: x̄ = Σmx/Σm = ∫x dm/∫dm.
The geometric centre of a line, area or volume, found with lengths, areas or volumes in place of weights: x̄ = ∫x dA/∫dA.
Q = ∫x dA about an axis, in mm³ (or m³); it is zero about any centroidal axis.
A thin flat plate of negligible thickness, so its weight can be treated as spread over an area.
For a shape given by a curve, x̄ = ∫x dA / ∫dA with dA taken as a thin strip of area, then integrated between limits.
Split the shape into standard pieces, take A and x̄ of each from a table, then x̄ = ΣAᵢxᵢ/ΣAᵢ; holes have negative area.
Surface area = curve length × distance moved by its centroid; volume = area × distance moved by its centroid, both for a full 2π sweep about an external axis.
I = ∫y² dA about an axis, in mm⁴; it measures how far the area lies from the axis.
J = ∫r² dA about a point O, in mm⁴, where r is the distance of the element from O.
I = I_c + A d², where I_c is about the centroidal axis parallel to the given axis, A is the area and d the gap between the axes.
For a thin flat area: J_z = I_x + I_y about the two in-plane axes and the axis normal to the plate at their crossing point.
k = √(I/A), the distance at which the whole area could sit and still give the same I; units mm.
I_xy = ∫xy dA, in mm⁴; it may be positive, negative or zero, and is zero for an axis of symmetry.
The pair of perpendicular centroidal axes for which the product of inertia is zero and the second moments are largest and smallest.
I₁,₂ = (I_x + I_y)/2 ± √[((I_x − I_y)/2)² + I_xy²], the extreme second moments of the area.
I = ∫r² dm = m k², in kg·m²; it is the resistance of a body to angular acceleration about the axis.
For mass moments, treat each standard solid with its own m and centroidal I, shift to the common axis by I = I_G + m d², and add.

takeaways: The centroid is only a weighted average of position: length-weighted for a wire, area-weighted for a lamina, mass-weighted for a solid.
When a boundary is a curve, that average turns into an integral; when the shape is made of standard pieces, it turns into an addition table with holes counted as negative areas.
Pappus-Guldinus converts one centroid calculation into a surface area or a volume, provided the sweep does not cut through the generating curve or area.
The second moment of area is a sum of area × distance², so material far from the axis counts far more than material near it — that is why an I-section beats a rectangle of the same area.
The parallel axis theorem lets you start from a centroidal value that is tabulated and shift it to any other parallel axis; the perpendicular axis theorem links J with I_x and I_y for a thin plate.
The radius of gyration turns a second moment into an equivalent distance, which makes comparisons between sections easy.
For every flat area there is a pair of principal axes at an angle θ_p = ½ tan⁻¹[−2I_xy/(I_x − I_y)] where I_xy vanishes and the second moments are extreme; I_x + I_y stays the same at every angle.
In dynamics the same distance-squared sum with masses gives the mass moment of inertia, and thin plates relate it to the area values through I_z = ρ t J_z.
Sketches, a clear table of elements and correct units (mm³ for first moments, mm⁴ for second moments, kg·m² for mass moments) carry most of the marks in this unit.
bank_note: Long answers here are nearly always numerical — a composite area or built-up section, a Pappus-Guldinus volume, and a mass moment of inertia of a composite body — so keep a labelled sketch, a table of elements with signs for holes, and units on every line.

bank.q: Distinguish between centre of gravity, centre of mass and centroid. Starting from the idea that the weight of a body acts through one point, derive the expressions for the centroid of a thin wire, a thin flat plate and a solid volume.
outline: Weight of an element = γA t; the resultant must act at a point for all orientations, so take moments about two axes
x̄ = ΣWx/ΣW gives the centre of gravity; dividing by g gives the centre of mass; setting density constant gives the centroid
Wire: replace A by length, x̄ = ΣLx/ΣL
Plate: x̄ = ∫x dA/∫dA, and similarly ȳ
Solid: replace dA by dV; state that a body with an axis of symmetry has its centroid on that axis

bank.q: State and prove the parallel axis theorem and the perpendicular axis theorem for a plane area. Give the conditions under which each is valid.
outline: Parallel: I about any axis = I about the parallel centroidal axis + A d²
Proof: take dA at (x, y) from centroidal axes, put I = ∫(y + d)² dA and expand; the cross term vanishes because ∫y dA = 0 about the centroid
Condition: the two axes must be parallel and one must pass through the centroid; d is the perpendicular gap
Perpendicular: I_z = I_x + I_y since r² = x² + y²
Condition: a thin flat plate, all three axes meeting at one point, z normal to the plate

bank.q: Define the second moment of area, the polar second moment of area and the radius of gyration. Write the values of I about the centroidal axes for a rectangle, a circle and a triangle, and explain why the second moment decides the bending stiffness of a beam.
outline: I = ∫y² dA, units mm⁴; J = ∫r² dA about a point
Rectangle: bd³/12 about the centroidal axis parallel to b; bd³/3 about the base
Circle: πd⁴/64 about a diameter, πd⁴/32 polar
Triangle: bh³/36 about the centroidal axis, bh³/12 about the base
Radius of gyration k = √(I/A); state the bending relation M/I = σ/y to link I with stress

bank.q: Explain the product of inertia of a plane area. Show that it is zero when one of the axes is an axis of symmetry, and define principal axes and principal moments of inertia.
outline: I_xy = ∫xy dA, sign depends on the quadrants occupied
For an axis of symmetry, each element at (x, y) pairs with one at (x, −y), so the sum cancels
Rotation of axes: I_x' = I_x cos²θ + I_y sin²θ − I_xy sin2θ, and I_x'y' = (I_x − I_y)sin2θ/2 + I_xy cos2θ
Principal axes are the θ_p where I_x'y' = 0, tan2θ_p = −2I_xy/(I_x − I_y)
Principal moments from I₁,₂ = (I_x + I_y)/2 ± √[((I_x − I_y)/2)² + I_xy²]

bank.q: Locate the centroid of a T-section with a flange 120 mm × 15 mm and a web 15 mm × 100 mm. Also find the centroid of an unequal angle section built from two such rectangles.
outline: Choose a reference line (bottom of the web) and draw the figure with dimensions
Table: piece, A, ȳ, Aȳ; two rows for the T-section
ΣA and ΣAȳ, then ȳ = ΣAȳ/ΣA; check the answer lies between the pieces' centroids
For the angle, use a similar table in both x and y
State units (mm) and give the distance from the stated reference

bank.q: Determine the centroid of a parabolic spandrel bounded by y = kx², the x-axis and x = a by integration. Also find the centroid of a quarter circle of radius r by integration.
outline: Take a vertical strip of width dx and height y; dA = y dx; element centroid at (x, y/2)
x̄ = ∫x y dx / ∫y dx between limits
ȳ = ∫(y/2) y dx / ∫y dx
For the spandrel get x̄ = 3a/4, ȳ = 3h/10 (h = ka²)
Quarter circle: use x̄ = ȳ = 4r/(3π) and show the strip integral

bank.q: Using the theorems of Pappus-Guldinus, find the volume and the surface area of a torus formed by rotating a circle of radius r about an axis in its plane at distance R from its centre (R > r). Also find the volume of a solid formed by rotating a semicircular area about its diameter.
outline: State both theorems and the condition that the axis must be external and not cut the generator
Curve length = 2πr, centroid travel = 2πR, so surface = 4π²rR
Area = πr², centroid travel = 2πR, so volume = 2π²r²R
Semicircle: area = πr²/2, centroid at 4r/(3π) from the diameter, so volume = (4/3)πr³
Sketch the generating curve, its centroid and the path of the centroid

bank.q: An I-section has flanges 150 mm × 20 mm and a web 200 mm × 15 mm, overall depth 240 mm. Find the second moment of area about the horizontal and vertical centroidal axes, the polar second moment about the centroid, and the radius of gyration about the horizontal axis.
outline: Locate the centroid first; for a doubly symmetric I-section the centroid is at the mid-depth
Table: piece, A, I_c of the piece, A d², total
I_xx = Σ(A d² + own centroidal I) about the horizontal centroidal axis
I_yy from the two flanges (web contributes little)
J = I_xx + I_yy by the perpendicular axis theorem
k = √(I_xx/A_total) in mm

bank.q: For a plane area, I_x = 12 × 10⁶ mm⁴, I_y = 4 × 10⁶ mm⁴ and I_xy = 3 × 10⁶ mm⁴ about centroidal axes. Find the principal moments of inertia and the directions of the principal axes. Verify that I_x + I_y is unchanged.
outline: Use I₁,₂ = (I_x + I_y)/2 ± √[((I_x − I_y)/2)² + I_xy²] with numbers
θ_p = ½ tan⁻¹[−2I_xy/(I_x − I_y)]; give the two values 90° apart
Identify which θ gives I₁ and which gives I₂
Check I₁ + I₂ = I_x + I_y
Comment: the larger principal moment corresponds to the axis about which the area is most spread

bank.q: Find the mass moment of inertia of a composite body made of a solid cylinder of mass m₁, radius r and height h, with a thin disc of mass m₂ and radius 2r fixed coaxially on top, about the common axis of symmetry.
outline: I_G of a cylinder about its own axis = m r²/2, independent of h
The disc has its centroid on the same axis, so no shift term is needed for this axis
Add: I = m₁r²/2 + m₂(2r)²/2
State units kg·m²; state that for an axis parallel to the base through the centre, I = m(3r² + h²)/12 and a shift would be needed
Sketch with dimensions labelled

bank.q: A rectangular plate of sides a and b, mass m, lies in the xy plane. Use the perpendicular axis theorem and the mass version of the parallel axis theorem to find its mass moment of inertia about (a) the centroidal axis normal to the plate, (b) an edge in the plane of the plate.
outline: For a thin plate the area and mass moments are linked: I_z(mass) = m J_z / A
J_z = (a² + b²)/12 for a rectangle about its centroid
So I_z = m(a² + b²)/12 about the normal centroidal axis
About an edge: I = m b²/3 for the axis along the other edge, from I_G = mb²/12 plus m(b/2)²
Show both the area route and the direct mass route give the same answer

bank.q: A rectangular beam 100 mm × 200 mm and an I-section of the same cross-sectional area are both used as simply supported beams of the same span and material. Analyse which gives the smaller bending stress for the same bending moment, and explain the role of the second moment of area in your answer.
outline: Bending stress σ = M y/I; for fixed M, a bigger I and a smaller y reduce stress
For the rectangle I = 100 × 200³/12 = 66.7 × 10⁶ mm⁴ with y = 100 mm
For the I-section of equal area, place most of the area in the flanges at large y
Show numerically that I of the I-section is much larger even though A is the same
Conclusion: stiffness depends on the distribution of area, not on its amount; state the practical limit (local buckling of thin webs is outside this analysis)

bank.q: A circular plate of radius R has a circular hole of radius R/2 cut in it, with the hole's centre at R/2 from the plate centre. Evaluate the shift in the centroid of the remaining area and its second moment about the horizontal centroidal axis, and state whether the hole increases or decreases I about that axis.
outline: Treat the hole as negative area; table with A, x̄, ȳ, A x̄, A ȳ
Centroid shifts towards the side opposite the hole; compute the distance
Find the centroidal axis of the remaining area first, then shift each piece to it
I of the full circle about the new axis minus I of the hole about the same axis
Comment on the sign of the result and on why a void can leave I almost unchanged if it lies near the centroid

bank.q: A flywheel for a small press is to store energy at a given speed. Compare a solid disc, a rim of the same mass concentrated at the outer radius, and a uniform plate of the same mass but a different radius, using mass moment of inertia. Recommend a shape and justify it in terms of energy stored and starting torque.
outline: Rotational kinetic energy = ½ I ω²; stored energy rises with I for a fixed ω
Disc: I = mR²/2; rim: I = mR²; the rim stores twice the energy for the same mass and outer radius
Discuss that the mass in hand is fixed, so only the radius of gyration k can be changed
Recommend a rim-weighted flywheel: large k, small starting torque penalty, safe stress
Mention that mass moment of inertia also fixes the angular acceleration for a given torque, τ = I α

glossary.def: The geometric centre of a line, area or volume, found as the position average of its elements weighted by length, area or volume.
The point through which the resultant weight of a body acts for every orientation of the body.
The point where the mass of a body may be treated as concentrated; it coincides with the centre of gravity where g is uniform.
The quantity ∫x dA or ∫y dA about an axis, measured in mm³, which vanishes about a centroidal axis.
A thin flat plate whose thickness is small enough to be neglected when finding its centroid or second moment.
A plane figure split into standard pieces such as rectangles, triangles and circles, some of which may be holes.
A rule giving the surface or volume swept by a curve or area rotated about an external coplanar axis, as length or area times the distance moved by the centroid.
The sum ∫y² dA of each element of area times the square of its distance from an axis, in mm⁴.
The sum ∫r² dA about a point, where r is the distance of each element from that point, equal to I_x + I_y for a thin plate.
The distance k = √(I/A) at which the whole area could be placed and still give the same second moment.
The rule I = I_c + A d² that shifts a second moment from a centroidal axis to a parallel axis a distance d away.
The rule J_z = I_x + I_y for a thin flat area, relating the polar second moment to two perpendicular in-plane second moments.
The quantity I_xy = ∫xy dA, measuring the lack of symmetry of an area about a pair of axes.
The perpendicular pair of axes through a point for which the product of inertia of the area is zero.
The largest and smallest second moments of an area, occurring about the principal axes and always adding up to I_x + I_y.
The sum ∫r² dm of each mass element times the square of its distance from an axis, in kg·m², the rotational counterpart of mass.
Any axis that passes through the centroid of the area or body; the second moment about it is the smallest for that direction.
A line such that the figure is its own mirror image across it; the product of inertia involving such an axis is zero.
The area between a curve such as a parabola and the coordinate axes, often used as an integration example for centroids.

glossary.term: Mohr's circle for moments of inertia
glossary.def: A graphical construction on axes of I and I_xy that gives the second moments about rotated axes and locates the principal axes visually.
A 3 × 3 array of second moments and products of inertia that fully describes the rotational inertia of a rigid body about any axis through a point.
A heavy rotating wheel whose large mass moment of inertia smooths out speed fluctuations in an engine or press.
The line in a bent beam cross-section where the bending stress is zero; it passes through the centroid of the section.
